scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that grants competition can motivate while arguing excess harms learning; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: In many classrooms, students work hard mainly to score higher than their classmates.
Some people believe that competition for high grades motivates students to excel, while others believe it seriously limits real learning.
I believe both views hold truth, though I lean toward the idea that moderate competition helps while excessive competition harms.
First, a healthy level of competition genuinely motivates students to do their best.
The wish to do well can push students to study harder and take their work seriously.
For example, a student may prepare more carefully simply to match the strong results of her classmates.
This shows that competition can raise effort and help students reach their full potential.
Comparing our work with others can also reveal how much we are truly capable of.
A little rivalry can make learning feel lively and exciting rather than dull.
To this extent, competition can be a real source of motivation.
Second, however, too much competition for grades can seriously damage real learning.
When only the score matters, students chase marks instead of genuine understanding.
Consider a student who crams facts for a test, passes it, and forgets everything a week later.
Such a focus shows that heavy competition can replace deep curiosity with a shallow hunt for grades.
Fear of falling behind can also discourage students from taking risks or helping one another.
Excessive competition can even turn classmates into rivals rather than partners in learning.
Beyond a certain point, then, competition begins to harm the very learning it should support.
In conclusion, a moderate amount of competition can genuinely motivate students to excel.
But excessive competition for grades can crush the curiosity that real learning requires.
The goal should be to use competition gently while keeping true understanding the highest prize.
